chunks: Typical SPI logic levels. The question: What are typical logic levels?
SPI does not define any voltage levels. The voltages are whatever the chips on the bus use. Each output drives its own supply voltage for a high and ground for a low.
When they differ, you must check each wire in its own direction, and you may need a level translator.
Imagine two people talking, each at their own volume. The supply voltage is how loud a person speaks.
A listener has a quietest sound they will still hear as a "yes", and a loudest sound they can take without being hurt.
If a loud speaker talks to a listener who can only handle quiet sounds, the listener is damaged.
If a quiet speaker talks to a listener who needs loud sounds, the message is missed.
A level translator is a go-between who repeats each message at the right volume, in both directions.
Three lines run master to slave (SCLK, MOSI, CS) and one runs the other way (MISO). The translator must be directional or auto-direction, and fast enough for the clock.
Each side's supply sets the logic levels on that side.
I/O supply: the voltage a chip's input and output pins run from. It sets that chip's high level. Input high threshold: the lowest voltage a receiver reliably reads as high.
It is often about 70% of its supply. Absolute maximum rating: the highest voltage a pin can see without damage. For many pins it is the supply plus about 0. 3 volts.
Level translator: a chip that converts signals between two supply voltages.
A 3. 3 volts microcontroller talks to a 1. 8 volts flash chip. The microcontroller's 3. 3 volts high goes into a flash pin that tolerates only about 2. 1 volts.
Going the other way, the flash's 1. 8 volts high must be read by the microcontroller, which needs 0. 7 times 3. 3 equals 2. 31 volts. So the flash's high may not be recognized.
Both directions fail, so you add a fast level translator. That is the whole idea.
"SPI defines no logic levels. It's push-pull CMOS at whatever the devices' I/O rails are, commonly 3. 3 volts, 1.
8 volts or 5 volts, with thresholds around 30% and 70% of the supply from each datasheet. Each output drives its own rail, unlike I2C where the pull-up sets the high.
If the two sides differ, check both directions against V IH and absolute maximum, and use a push-pull level translator fast enough for the clock, with MISO going the other way."
Quick check. A 1. 8 volts flash drives MISO into a 3. 3 volts MCU whose V IH equals 0. 7 volts DD . What happens?
